{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_c70213cb96294ac2b000f8d5","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# gribtract Plan\n2\t\n3\t## Overview\n4\t\n5\tA pure-Rust GRIB2 decoder that turns NOAA/WMO GRIB2 messages into typed metadata\n6\tand gridded numeric data, gated at every step on field-by-field agreement with a\n7\treference decoder (eccodes / wgrib2) over a corpus of real NOAA products.\n8\t\n9\tThis is an **oracle-first** project. The differential harness is built before the\n10\tdecoder is \"done,\" so that autonomous (marathon) coding sessions always have a\n11\tconcrete, externally-verifiable hill to climb: *find a message gribtract decodes\n12\twrong → add it as a fixture → fix the decode → harness confirms no regression →\n13\trepeat.*\n14\t\n15\t## Design principles\n16\t\n17\t1. **The oracle is the product.** The decoder is only as trustworthy as the\n18\t   corpus and the differential check behind it. Harness work is never \"overhead.\"\n19\t2. **Real files only.** Fixtures are actual NOAA grib2 messages (GFS, HRRR, NBM,\n20\t   GEFS, …), not synthetic. An upstream archive already captures these — seed from it.\n21\t3. **Tolerance is derived, not guessed.** Grid-value equality is checked within\n22\t   the precision implied by the packing template (e.g. decimal/binary scale\n23\t   factors), not a magic epsilon. The tolerance policy is documented and tested.\n24\t4. **Every disagreement becomes a permanent fixture.** Monotonic improvement; the\n25\t   regression ratchet is the whole point.\n26\t5. **Sub-minute verify.** `cargo test` (local, cgroup-limited or CI) must run\n27\t   the full differential suite fast enough to drive an unattended loop. Large\n28\t   corpora are sharded/sampled in the fast path, exhaustive in CI.\n29\t\n30\t## Architecture\n31\t\n32\t```\n33\t                 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n34\t   .grib2 bytes  │  gribtract-core (no_std-friendly where able)  │\n35\t   ───────────►  │                                                │\n36\t                 │  Indicator(0) → Identification(1) → Local(2)   │\n37\t                 │   → Grid Def(3) → Product Def(4)               │\n38\t                 │   → Data Representation(5) → Bitmap(6)          │\n39\t                 │   → Data(7) → End(8)                           │\n40\t                 │                                                │\n41\t                 │  section split → template dispatch → unpack    │\n42\t                 └───────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘\n43\t                                 │ Vec<Field { meta, grid, values }>\n44\t                 ┌───────────────▼───────────────┐\n45\t                 │  gribtract (high-level API)    │  iterate messages,\n46\t                 │  + CLI (`gribtract decode`)    │  select by key, dump JSON\n47\t                 └───────────────┬───────────────┘\n48\t                                 │\n49\t          ┌──────────────────────▼───────────────────────┐\n50\t          │  differential harness (tests/ + xtask)         │\n51\t          │  gribtract vs eccodes/wgrib2 over corpus       │\n52\t          │  → field-by-field + grid-within-tolerance      │\n53\t          └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n54\t```\n55\t\n56\t### Crate layout (workspace)\n57\t\n58\t- `crates/gribtract-core` — section parsing, template dispatch, unpacking. No I/O.\n59\t- `crates/gribtract` — high-level message iterator, field selection, public API.\n60\t- `crates/gribtract-cli` — `gribtract decode|list|dump` (JSON/CSV out).\n61\t- `crates/gribtract-testutil` — shared test utilities and fixtures for differential testing.\n62\t- `crates/gribtract-py` — Python bindings via PyO3.\n63\t- `crates/gribtract-fetch` — HTTP byte-range fetching for GRIB2 files with provider probing.\n64\t- `xtask` — corpus management, reference-decoder runner, tolerance reports.\n65\t- `crates/gribtract/tests/` — differential conformance suite (differential.rs, station_extraction.rs).\n66\t\n67\t## Components\n68\t\n69\t### Section parser\n70\tSplits a GRIB2 message into sections 0–8, validates length/number fields, supports\n71\tmulti-field messages (repeated sections 2–7) and the GRIB2 \"edition 2\" framing.\n72\t\n73\t### Template registry\n74\tGRIB2's complexity lives in three template families. Each gets a registry mapping\n75\ttemplate number → decoder:\n76\t- **Grid Definition Templates (3.x)** — lat/lon, Lambert conformal, polar\n77\t  stereographic, Gaussian, rotated grids. Determines point geometry.\n78\t- **Product Definition Templates (4.x)** — what the field *is* (parameter, level,\n79\t  forecast time, ensemble member, statistical processing).\n80\t- **Data Representation Templates (5.x)** — how values are packed: simple, complex,\n81\t  complex+spatial-differencing, IEEE float, JPEG2000, PNG.\n82\t\n83\t### Unpackers\n84\tThe hard numeric core. Per data-representation template: read reference value,\n85\tbinary/decimal scale, bit-depth; expand bitmap; apply scaling; (for 5.40/5.41)\n86\tJPEG2000/PNG decode; (for 5.3) spatial differencing reversal.\n87\t\n88\t### Differential harness\n89\tRuns both decoders over the corpus, compares metadata exactly and grid values\n90\twithin derived tolerance, emits a per-template coverage + agreement report.\n91\t\n92\t### Throughput & proof-of-speed dashboard\n93\tA self-contained HTML dashboard that **proves gribtract decodes at the claimed\n94\tspeed, on real files, reproducibly** — and shows it next to correctness so speed\n95\tis never claimed without proof of a correct decode. Fed by a machine-readable\n96\t`bench-results.json` emitted by the benchmark harness (`cargo run --bin xtask -- bench`),\n97\tnever hand-edited. See `docs/notes/throughput-dashboard.md` for the full spec.\n98\tThis is the artifact that answers \"is it actually working at that speed?\" — it is\n99\ta deliverable, not an afterthought, and is wired in early (Phase 2) so every later\n100\titeration updates it.\n101\t\n102\t### Provider probe & selection\n103\t\n104\tgribtract's fetch layer (Phase 7) must retrieve GRIB2 files from one of several\n105\tupstream providers that mirror the same NOAA data with different latency and\n106\tthroughput characteristics depending on deployment location:\n107\t\n108\t| Provider | Hosts | Notes |\n109\t|----------|-------|-------|\n110\t| NOAA S3 | `noaa-gfs-bdp-pds`, `noaa-hrrr-bdp-pds`, `noaa-gefs-pds`, `noaa-nbm-grib2-pds` (all us-east-1) | Direct regional endpoint; no CDN; ~10ms from US east coast, ~100ms from Europe |\n111\t| Google Cloud Storage | `high-resolution-rapid-refresh`, `national-blend-of-models`, `gfs-ensemble-forecast-system` | CDN-fronted; ~3–5ms connect anywhere; TTFB still ~110–290ms depending on distance to US origin |\n112\t| NOMADS | `nomads.ncep.noaa.gov` | CDN-fronted HTTP; index + range-request capable; good TTFB fallback |\n113\t\n114\tThe optimal provider is **per-model and per-deployment** — e.g. a Europe-based host\n115\tshould prefer GCS for HRRR + NBM (CDN gives 3ms connect vs 100ms S3) while a\n116\tUS-east host should prefer S3 for GFS + NBM (direct 11ms connect, 375ms TTFB vs\n117\tGCS's 112ms). Hardcoding a provider is fragile; instead, gribtract probes at\n118\tstartup and caches the result.\n119\t\n120\t**Probe mechanism (`xtask probe-providers` / runtime `ProviderProbe`):**\n121\t\n122\t1. For each (model, provider) pair, issue a small representative request:\n123\t   a. Fetch the `.idx` index file (a few KB, always text) for a recent known cycle.\n124\t   b. Issue one HTTP range request for the first message in that index (validates\n125\t      both connectivity and range-request support end-to-end).\n126\t2. Record: TCP connect time, TTFB, bytes-per-second for the range payload.\n127\t3. Rank providers per model by a combined score: `connect_ms + ttfb_ms + 1000/throughput_mbs`.\n128\t4. Write results to `provider-probe.json` (alongside `bench-results.json`).\n129\t5. At runtime, the fetch layer loads `provider-probe.json` on startup and falls\n130\t   back to re-probing live if the file is absent, stale (>24h), or if a provider\n131\t   returns HTTP errors on N consecutive requests.\n132\t\n133\t**Probe is non-blocking for decoding.** The library itself (gribtract-core,\n134\tgribtract) has zero network dependencies. The probe lives in `xtask` and in an\n135\toptional `gribtract-fetch` crate that the CLI and downstream integrations opt in to.\n136\t\n137\t### Fixed-station point-extraction benchmark\n138\tA second benchmark workload alongside bulk full-grid decode: extract a per-station\n139\t**time series** (one value per forecast hour, across a cycle) at a fixed roster of\n140\t20 US metropolitan METAR station coordinates — the common \"I only need the value at\n141\tthese points, across the horizon\" hot path. It measures `stations × hours / sec`\n142\tfrom raw bytes to assembled matrix, in nearest and bilinear modes, each verified\n143\tagainst the full-grid decode at the same points. This is deliberately an **open-\n144\tended optimization target**: decoding a whole grid to read a few points is wasteful,\n145\tbut GRIB2 packing makes cheap random access hard, so there is a long tail of\n146\ttechniques to try — many will be dead ends, and that is expected. See\n147\t`docs/notes/station-extraction-benchmark.md`.\n148\t\n149\t## Data Models\n150\t\n151\t```rust\n152\tstruct Message<'a> { sections: Sections<'a>, fields: Vec<Field> }\n153\t\n154\tstruct Field {\n155\t    discipline: u8,\n156\t    parameter: ParameterId,      // category + number → name/units\n157\t    level: Level,                // type + value(s)\n158\t    forecast: ForecastTime,      // reference time + offset + statistical window\n159\t    ensemble: Option<Ensemble>,  // member / type\n160\t    grid: GridDefinition,        // template 3.x → geometry + point order\n161\t    values: GridValues,          // f64 grid + missing mask\n162\t}\n163\t\n164\tenum GridValues { Dense(Vec<f64>), Masked { values: Vec<f64>, present: BitVec } }\n165\t```\n166\t\n167\t### Benchmark result (drives the dashboard)\n168\t\n169\t```jsonc\n170\t// bench-results.json — one record per benchmarked decode run\n171\t{\n172\t  \"git_sha\": \"…\", \"timestamp\": \"…\",          // provenance, stamped by xtask\n173\t  \"host\": { \"cpu\": \"…\", \"cores\": 8, \"mem_gb\": 62 },\n174\t  \"corpus\": { \"name\": \"gfs-2026-06\", \"messages\": 4096, \"bytes\": 1734967296 },\n175\t  \"runs\": [\n176\t    { \"decoder\": \"gribtract\", \"template_5x\": \"5.3\",\n177\t      \"messages_per_sec\": 0, \"mb_per_sec\": 0, \"grid_points_per_sec\": 0,\n178\t      \"wall_ms\": 0, \"agreement\": 1.0 },          // correctness rides alongside speed\n179\t    { \"decoder\": \"eccodes\",  \"template_5x\": \"5.3\", \"mb_per_sec\": 0, \"wall_ms\": 0 },\n180\t    { \"decoder\": \"wgrib2\",   \"template_5x\": \"5.3\", \"mb_per_sec\": 0, \"wall_ms\": 0 }\n181\t  ]\n182\t}\n183\t```\n184\t\n185\tSpeedup vs. each reference decoder is computed from these records; the dashboard\n186\trenders the comparison and the absolute throughput, both tagged with `git_sha` +\n187\t`host` so a claimed number is always reproducible and attributable.\n188\t\n189\t## Implementation Phases\n190\t\n191\t- [x] **Phase 0 — Oracle harness first.** Stand up the corpus loader, the\n192\t  eccodes/wgrib2 reference runner (on a host with the reference toolchain installed),\n193\t  the field-by-field comparator, and the tolerance policy. Wire `cargo test` to run\n194\t  a sampled differential suite. *Deliverable: a failing-but-green-framework that\n195\t  can score any decoder against the corpus.*\n196\t- [x] **Phase 1 — Framing + metadata.** Section 0–8 split, identification/grid/\n197\t  product metadata. Match all non-value fields exactly for GFS surface temp.\n198\t- [x] **Phase 2 — Simple packing (5.0) + lat/lon grid (3.0).** First end-to-end\n199\t  numeric agreement on the most common GFS/NBM fields.\n200\t- [x] **Phase 2b — Proof-of-speed dashboard (wired in here, updated forever after).**\n201\t  Benchmark harness emits `bench-results.json` (throughput + agreement, vs\n202\t  eccodes/wgrib2); self-contained HTML dashboard renders it with a live `--serve`\n203\t  mode. From here on, every phase's work must keep the dashboard green and current.\n204\t  See `docs/notes/throughput-dashboard.md`.\n205\t- [ ] **Phase 2c — Point-extraction parse-speed track (ongoing, never \"done\").**\n206\t  Add the fixed-station point-extraction benchmark (`stations × hours / sec`,\n207\t  nearest + bilinear, each verified against full-grid decode at the points), then\n208\t  **iterate on parse speed indefinitely** — lazy/partial unpack, geometry +\n209\t  bitmap-rank caches reused across forecast hours, SIMD spans, decode-once-extract-\n210\t  many, parallelism, zero-copy slicing, and techniques not yet thought of. **Expect\n211\t  many dead ends and failed attempts — that is the point of the track.** A technique\n212\t  that proves *not* to help is a valid iteration: record it in the techniques log so\n213\t  the loop doesn't re-walk it. The only hard rule is the project's rule — correctness\n214\t  gates speed; a faster path that changes a value is a regression, not progress.\n215\t  See `docs/notes/station-extraction-benchmark.md`. This track runs in parallel with\n216\t  the phases below and is never checked off.\n217\t- [x] **Phase 3 — Complex packing (5.2/5.3) + spatial differencing.** Unlocks most\n218\t  HRRR fields. The numerically trickiest unpacker.\n219\t- [x] **Phase 4 — JPEG2000 (5.40) + PNG (5.41).** Compressed grids (common in some\n220\t  NOAA products). Pull in a Rust j2k/png path.\n221\t- [x] **Phase 5 — Grid geometry breadth.** Lambert conformal (HRRR native), polar\n222\t  stereographic, Gaussian, rotated. Geometry must match for point asof-joins.\n223\t- [x] **Phase 6 — Ensembles + statistical products (GEFS).** Product templates for\n224\t  members and time-aggregated fields.\n225\t- [ ] **Phase 7 — Publish + integrate.** crates.io, Python bindings, and the\n226\t  forecast-timeseries emitter consumed by downstream time-series analysis.\n227\t  Includes the **provider probe** (`xtask probe-providers` + runtime `ProviderProbe`):\n228\t  each candidate provider for each model is probed at startup (`.idx` fetch + one\n229\t  range request); results cached to `provider-probe.json` with a 24h TTL. See the\n230\t  \"Provider probe & selection\" component above for the full spec.\n231\t\n232\t  **Status (2026-07-27):** Python bindings (gribtract-py) and provider probe are\n233\t  implemented. crates.io publish prep is complete (docs/notes/publish-guide.md,\n234\t  dry-run verified), but the actual publish step requires a crates.io API token\n235\t  — an ExternalSecret following the `crates-io-token-pdftract-externalsecret.yml.disabled`\n236\t  pattern needs to be provisioned in declarative-config, then the publish sequence\n237\t  in publish-guide.md must be run by a maintainer. Neither `gribtract` nor\n238\t  `gribtract-core` is currently live on crates.io (verified via crates.io API).\n239\t\n240\t## Marathon loop contract\n241\t\n242\tFor an autonomous session to make safe, monotonic progress, each iteration must:\n243\t1. Pick a corpus message currently failing (or absent) — the harness lists them.\n244\t2. Add/confirm it as a fixture (real file, provenance recorded).\n245\t3. Implement/repair the relevant template decoder.\n246\t4. `cargo test` → full sampled differential suite passes; no regression vs the\n247\t   ratcheted fixture set.\n248\t5. Commit. The loop drives two coupled north-star metrics upward, **in this\n249\t   priority**: (a) **agreement coverage** (% messages matching, by template) — the\n250\t   gate; and (b) **decode throughput** (MB/s and speedup vs eccodes/wgrib2, plus\n251\t   `stations × hours / sec` for point extraction) — the proof. A throughput gain\n252\t   that lowers agreement is a regression, not progress. Both are published to the\n253\t   proof-of-speed dashboard every iteration.\n254\t\n255\tSeparately from the phase work, the **point-extraction parse-speed track (Phase 2c)\n256\tis an open-ended optimization loop**: keep trying new techniques to make station\n257\textraction faster, expect most attempts to fail or regress and back them out, and\n258\tlog what didn't work so the loop doesn't repeat it. Dead ends are normal here — the\n259\tcorrectness gate makes the exploration safe. When no template/correctness bead is\n260\tthe obvious next pick, advancing this track is always valid work.\n261\t\n262\t## Open Questions\n263\t\n264\t- **Reference decoder of record:** eccodes (richer metadata) vs wgrib2 (ubiquitous\n265\t  in NOAA tooling)? Likely eccodes primary, wgrib2 as a second cross-check.\n266\t- **Tolerance derivation:** confirm that decimal/binary scale factors fully\n267\t  determine representable precision for each packing template, or whether some\n268\t  templates need an empirically-set band.\n269\t- **Corpus governance:** fixtures are real grib2 — size/licensing/storage. Store\n270\t  large fixtures out-of-tree (B2) with a manifest + hash, fetched by the harness?\n271\t- **JPEG2000 in Rust:** is there a pure-Rust J2K decoder of sufficient fidelity,\n272\t  or is a vetted FFI dependency acceptable for template 5.40 only?\n273\t- **Where the reference runs:** the differential harness needs the C toolchain;\n274\t  run it on a host with the reference toolchain installed. CI wiring TBD.\n275\t- **Scope of metadata naming:** ship a parameter/level name table, or expose raw\n276\t  numeric ids and leave naming to the consumer initially?\n277\t\n278\t## ADR-1: 2026-07-20 — Add a wasm32 build target and a public, client-side interactive decode demo\n279\t\n280\t### Context\n281\t\n282\tgribtract's core value proposition, stated in the README, is \"no C toolchain, no\n283\tFFI\" for the default build (DRT 5.0/5.2/5.3/5.41 — JPEG2000 is the one deliberate,\n284\tfeature-gated exception). `gribtract-core` is already described in\n285\t`docs/plan/plan.md` as \"no_std-friendly where able\" and has zero I/O dependencies —\n286\tit takes `&[u8]` in, returns typed `Field`s out.\n287\t\n288\tDespite that, the only way anyone can currently *experience* gribtract is `git\n289\tclone` + `cargo build`. The repo is public (6 GitHub stargazers as of 2026-07-20),\n290\tnot yet published to crates.io (`bf-1pyo` closed its dry-run work but the actual\n291\t`cargo publish` step is blocked on a maintainer-held crates.io token that does not\n292\texist on this box — flagged as a blocker below, not solved by this ADR), and the\n293\tproof-of-speed dashboard (`dashboard.html` + `bench-results.json`, see \"Throughput &\n294\tproof-of-speed dashboard\" above) only renders locally via `cargo xtask serve`. For a\n295\tproject trying to earn adoption, \"clone a Rust workspace and compile it\" is a lot to\n296\task of someone evaluating whether gribtract solves their problem. There is currently\n297\tno zero-install way to hand someone a `.grib2` file's worth of proof that this\n298\tworks.\n299\t\n300\tMeanwhile, decode is demonstrably fast and self-contained (100+ MB/s on simple\n301\tpacking per `bench-results.json`, all reference-decoder-verified) and the crate\n302\tboundary (`gribtract-core` → `gribtract`) already separates the pure-computation\n303\tpath from I/O concerns (`gribtract-fetch`) and from platform-specific bindings\n304\t(`gribtract-py`). WebAssembly is a natural next target: it is, by construction, the\n305\tstrictest possible \"no C toolchain, no FFI, no host filesystem\" execution\n306\tenvironment — running gribtract-core in a browser tab is not just a demo gimmick,\n307\tit is a forcing function that structurally enforces the project's core claim.\n308\t\n309\t### Decision\n310\t\n311\tAdd `wasm32-unknown-unknown` as a first-class, CI-checked build target for\n312\t`gribtract-core` and `gribtract` (the pure-compute crates only — `gribtract-fetch`\n313\tand `gribtract-py` are explicitly out of scope for wasm), via a new thin wrapper\n314\tcrate `crates/gribtract-wasm` (wasm-bindgen bindings exposing `decode(bytes: &[u8])\n315\t-> JsValue` and a lazy point-extraction call). Ship a small, self-contained static\n316\tHTML page — same \"no external CDN at runtime, opens offline\" rule already\n317\testablished for `dashboard.html` in `docs/notes/throughput-dashboard.md` — that lets\n318\ta visitor drag a `.grib2` file onto the page and see it decoded live in their\n319\tbrowser: a field inventory table plus a simple canvas heatmap of one selected\n320\tfield's grid. No server, no upload, no install. This becomes the project's public\n321\tfront door: the README's and repo's primary \"try it\" link, replacing \"clone and\n322\t`cargo build --release`\" as the first thing an evaluator is asked to do.\n323\t\n324\tThis is implemented as follow-on beads (see below), not in this commit — this ADR\n325\trecords the decision to take the dependency-shape and target-support hit, and why.\n326\t\n327\t### Alternatives Considered\n328\t\n329\t1. **Status quo — Rust crate + CLI only.** Zero extra maintenance surface. Rejected\n330\t   as insufficient for a public repo trying to earn adoption before it is even on\n331\t   crates.io: the only path to \"does this work for my file?\" is a full Rust\n332\t   toolchain and a `cargo build`, which is a high floor for a first impression.\n333\t2. **Host only the existing proof-of-speed dashboard publicly, skip wasm.** Cheaper\n334\t   — reuses `dashboard.html` as-is, and does prove the speed claim publicly. But it\n335\t   is a *report*, not a *demo*: a visitor still cannot bring their own file and see\n336\t   it decoded. Complementary, not a substitute — filed as its own bead\n337\t   (`artifact-improvement`, \"publish the proof-of-speed dashboard as a live site\")\n338\t   rather than folded into this decision.\n339\t3. **Server-side decode API (upload a file, get JSON back) instead of client-side\n340\t   wasm.** Rejected: reintroduces a server, hosting cost, and an upload/attack\n341\t   surface for a project whose entire selling point is \"no dependencies, runs\n342\t   anywhere.\" Client-side wasm keeps decode fully in the visitor's browser — zero\n343\t   backend, zero file upload, consistent with \"pure-Rust, no C toolchain\" extended\n344\t   one step further to \"no server, either.\"\n345\t4. **Lead with the Python bindings (`gribtract-py`, already planned for Phase 7) as\n346\t   the primary \"try it\" path instead.** Rejected as the *primary* surface — `pip\n347\t   install` + a Python runtime is still real friction compared to a link that opens\n348\t   in any browser. The PyO3 bindings remain valuable as a separate, already-planned\n349\t   deliverable; they don't substitute for a zero-install public demo.\n350\t\n351\t### Consequences\n352\t\n353\t- New crate `crates/gribtract-wasm` added to the workspace (wasm-bindgen dependency,\n354\t  `cdylib` crate-type, mirroring the existing `gribtract-py` pattern of an\n355\t  optional/non-default workspace member so default `cargo build`/`cargo test`\n356\t  behavior is unaffected).\n357\t- `wasm32-unknown-unknown` becomes a second target the differential-harness\n358\t  contract implicitly protects: `gribtract-core`'s \"no_std-friendly where able\"\n359\t  note goes from aspirational to load-bearing. Any future dependency added to\n360\t  `gribtract-core` or `gribtract` that breaks a `cargo build --target\n361\t  wasm32-unknown-unknown -p gribtract` check is a regression, the same way a\n362\t  differential-agreement drop is a regression.\n363\t- Wasm binary size becomes a metric worth tracking (small today given\n364\t  `gribtract-core`'s minimal dependency footprint) — a follow-on bead should add a\n365\t  size check alongside the existing throughput/agreement metrics so it doesn't\n366\t  silently creep.\n367\t- Does **not** touch the correctness oracle or the Phase 2c parse-speed track: the\n368\t  wasm target compiles the same `gribtract-core` source the differential harness\n369\t  already verifies, so existing agreement guarantees carry over unchanged. The differential harness is built before the\ndecoder is \"done,\" so that autonomous (marathon) coding sessions always have a\nconcrete, externally-verifiable hill to climb: *find a message gribtract decodes\nwrong → add it as a fixture → fix the decode → harness confirms no regression →\nrepeat.*\n\n## Design principles\n\n1. **The oracle is the product.** The decoder is only as trustworthy as the\n   corpus and the differential check behind it. Harness work is never \"overhead.\"\n2. **Real files only.** Fixtures are actual NOAA grib2 messages (GFS, HRRR, NBM,\n   GEFS, …), not synthetic. An upstream archive already captures these — seed from it.\n3. **Tolerance is derived, not guessed.** Grid-value equality is checked within\n   the precision implied by the packing template (e.g. decimal/binary scale\n   factors), not a magic epsilon. The tolerance policy is documented and tested.\n4. **Every disagreement becomes a permanent fixture.** Monotonic improvement; the\n   regression ratchet is the whole point.\n5. **Sub-minute verify.** `cargo test` (local, cgroup-limited or CI) must run\n   the full differential suite fast enough to drive an unattended loop. Large\n   corpora are sharded/sampled in the fast path, exhaustive in CI.\n\n## Architecture\n\n```\n                 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n   .grib2 bytes  │  gribtract-core (no_std-friendly where able)  │\n   ───────────►  │                                                │\n                 │  Indicator(0) → Identification(1) → Local(2)   │\n                 │   → Grid Def(3) → Product Def(4)               │\n                 │   → Data Representation(5) → Bitmap(6)          │\n                 │   → Data(7) → End(8)                           │\n                 │                                                │\n                 │  section split → template dispatch → unpack    │\n                 └───────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘\n                                 │ Vec<Field { meta, grid, values }>\n                 ┌───────────────▼───────────────┐\n                 │  gribtract (high-level API)    │  iterate messages,\n                 │  + CLI (`gribtract decode`)    │  select by key, dump JSON\n                 └───────────────┬───────────────┘\n                                 │\n          ┌──────────────────────▼───────────────────────┐\n          │  differential harness (tests/ + xtask)         │\n          │  gribtract vs eccodes/wgrib2 over corpus       │\n          │  → field-by-field + grid-within-tolerance      │\n          └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n### Crate layout (workspace)\n\n- `crates/gribtract-core` — section parsing, template dispatch, unpacking. No I/O.\n- `crates/gribtract` — high-level message iterator, field selection, public API.\n- `crates/gribtract-cli` — `gribtract decode|list|dump` (JSON/CSV out).\n- `crates/gribtract-testutil` — shared test utilities and fixtures for differential testing.\n- `crates/gribtract-py` — Python bindings via PyO3.\n- `crates/gribtract-fetch` — HTTP byte-range fetching for GRIB2 files with provider probing.\n- `xtask` — corpus management, reference-decoder runner, tolerance reports.\n- `crates/gribtract/tests/` — differential conformance suite (differential.rs, station_extraction.rs).\n\n## Components\n\n### Section parser\nSplits a GRIB2 message into sections 0–8, validates length/number fields, supports\nmulti-field messages (repeated sections 2–7) and the GRIB2 \"edition 2\" framing.\n\n### Template registry\nGRIB2's complexity lives in three template families. Each gets a registry mapping\ntemplate number → decoder:\n- **Grid Definition Templates (3.x)** — lat/lon, Lambert conformal, polar\n  stereographic, Gaussian, rotated grids. Determines point geometry.\n- **Product Definition Templates (4.x)** — what the field *is* (parameter, level,\n  forecast time, ensemble member, statistical processing).\n- **Data Representation Templates (5.x)** — how values are packed: simple, complex,\n  complex+spatial-differencing, IEEE float, JPEG2000, PNG.\n\n### Unpackers\nThe hard numeric core. Per data-representation template: read reference value,\nbinary/decimal scale, bit-depth; expand bitmap; apply scaling; (for 5.40/5.41)\nJPEG2000/PNG decode; (for 5.3) spatial differencing reversal.\n\n### Differential harness\nRuns both decoders over the corpus, compares metadata exactly and grid values\nwithin derived tolerance, emits a per-template coverage + agreement report.\n\n### Throughput & proof-of-speed dashboard\nA self-contained HTML dashboard that **proves gribtract decodes at the claimed\nspeed, on real files, reproducibly** — and shows it next to correctness so speed\nis never claimed without proof of a correct decode. Fed by a machine-readable\n`bench-results.json` emitted by the benchmark harness (`cargo run --bin xtask -- bench`),\nnever hand-edited. See `docs/notes/throughput-dashboard.md` for the full spec.\nThis is the artifact that answers \"is it actually working at that speed?\" — it is\na deliverable, not an afterthought, and is wired in early (Phase 2) so every later\niteration updates it.\n\n### Provider probe & selection\n\ngribtract's fetch layer (Phase 7) must retrieve GRIB2 files from one of several\nupstream providers that mirror the same NOAA data with different latency and\nthroughput characteristics depending on deployment location:\n\n| Provider | Hosts | Notes |\n|----------|-------|-------|\n| NOAA S3 | `noaa-gfs-bdp-pds`, `noaa-hrrr-bdp-pds`, `noaa-gefs-pds`, `noaa-nbm-grib2-pds` (all us-east-1) | Direct regional endpoint; no CDN; ~10ms from US east coast, ~100ms from Europe |\n| Google Cloud Storage | `high-resolution-rapid-refresh`, `national-blend-of-models`, `gfs-ensemble-forecast-system` | CDN-fronted; ~3–5ms connect anywhere; TTFB still ~110–290ms depending on distance to US origin |\n| NOMADS | `nomads.ncep.noaa.gov` | CDN-fronted HTTP; index + range-request capable; good TTFB fallback |\n\nThe optimal provider is **per-model and per-deployment** — e.g. a Europe-based host\nshould prefer GCS for HRRR + NBM (CDN gives 3ms connect vs 100ms S3) while a\nUS-east host should prefer S3 for GFS + NBM (direct 11ms connect, 375ms TTFB vs\nGCS's 112ms). Hardcoding a provider is fragile; instead, gribtract probes at\nstartup and caches the result.\n\n**Probe mechanism (`xtask probe-providers` / runtime `ProviderProbe`):**\n\n1. For each (model, provider) pair, issue a small representative request:\n   a. Fetch the `.idx` index file (a few KB, always text) for a recent known cycle.\n   b. Issue one HTTP range request for the first message in that index (validates\n      both connectivity and range-request support end-to-end).\n2. Record: TCP connect time, TTFB, bytes-per-second for the range payload.\n3. Rank providers per model by a combined score: `connect_ms + ttfb_ms + 1000/throughput_mbs`.\n4. Write results to `provider-probe.json` (alongside `bench-results.json`).\n5. At runtime, the fetch layer loads `provider-probe.json` on startup and falls\n   back to re-probing live if the file is absent, stale (>24h), or if a provider\n   returns HTTP errors on N consecutive requests.\n\n**Probe is non-blocking for decoding.** The library itself (gribtract-core,\ngribtract) has zero network dependencies. The probe lives in `xtask` and in an\noptional `gribtract-fetch` crate that the CLI and downstream integrations opt in to.\n\n### Fixed-station point-extraction benchmark\nA second benchmark workload alongside bulk full-grid decode: extract a per-station\n**time series** (one value per forecast hour, across a cycle) at a fixed roster of\n20 US metropolitan METAR station coordinates — the common \"I only need the value at\nthese points, across the horizon\" hot path. It measures `stations × hours / sec`\nfrom raw bytes to assembled matrix, in nearest and bilinear modes, each verified\nagainst the full-grid decode at the same points. This is deliberately an **open-\nended optimization target**: decoding a whole grid to read a few points is wasteful,\nbut GRIB2 packing makes cheap random access hard, so there is a long tail of\ntechniques to try — many will be dead ends, and that is expected. See\n`docs/notes/station-extraction-benchmark.md`.\n\n## Data Models\n\n```rust\nstruct Message<'a> { sections: Sections<'a>, fields: Vec<Field> }\n\nstruct Field {\n    discipline: u8,\n    parameter: ParameterId,      // category + number → name/units\n    level: Level,                // type + value(s)\n    forecast: ForecastTime,      // reference time + offset + statistical window\n    ensemble: Option<Ensemble>,  // member / type\n    grid: GridDefinition,        // template 3.x → geometry + point order\n    values: GridValues,          // f64 grid + missing mask\n}\n\nenum GridValues { Dense(Vec<f64>), Masked { values: Vec<f64>, present: BitVec } }\n```\n\n### Benchmark result (drives the dashboard)\n\n```jsonc\n// bench-results.json — one record per benchmarked decode run\n{\n  \"git_sha\": \"…\", \"timestamp\": \"…\",          // provenance, stamped by xtask\n  \"host\": { \"cpu\": \"…\", \"cores\": 8, \"mem_gb\": 62 },\n  \"corpus\": { \"name\": \"gfs-2026-06\", \"messages\": 4096, \"bytes\": 1734967296 },\n  \"runs\": [\n    { \"decoder\": \"gribtract\", \"template_5x\": \"5.3\",\n      \"messages_per_sec\": 0, \"mb_per_sec\": 0, \"grid_points_per_sec\": 0,\n      \"wall_ms\": 0, \"agreement\": 1.0 },          // correctness rides alongside speed\n    { \"decoder\": \"eccodes\",  \"template_5x\": \"5.3\", \"mb_per_sec\": 0, \"wall_ms\": 0 },\n    { \"decoder\": \"wgrib2\",   \"template_5x\": \"5.3\", \"mb_per_sec\": 0, \"wall_ms\": 0 }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nSpeedup vs. each reference decoder is computed from these records; the dashboard\nrenders the comparison and the absolute throughput, both tagged with `git_sha` +\n`host` so a claimed number is always reproducible and attributable.\n\n## Implementation Phases\n\n- [x] **Phase 0 — Oracle harness first.** Stand up the corpus loader, the\n  eccodes/wgrib2 reference runner (on a host with the reference toolchain installed),\n  the field-by-field comparator, and the tolerance policy. From here on, every phase's work must keep the dashboard green and current.\n  See `docs/notes/throughput-dashboard.md`.\n- [ ] **Phase 2c — Point-extraction parse-speed track (ongoing, never \"done\").**\n  Add the fixed-station point-extraction benchmark (`stations × hours / sec`,\n  nearest + bilinear, each verified against full-grid decode at the points), then\n  **iterate on parse speed indefinitely** — lazy/partial unpack, geometry +\n  bitmap-rank caches reused across forecast hours, SIMD spans, decode-once-extract-\n  many, parallelism, zero-copy slicing, and techniques not yet thought of. **Expect\n  many dead ends and failed attempts — that is the point of the track.** A technique\n  that proves *not* to help is a valid iteration: record it in the techniques log so\n  the loop doesn't re-walk it. The only hard rule is the project's rule — correctness\n  gates speed; a faster path that changes a value is a regression, not progress.\n  See `docs/notes/station-extraction-benchmark.md`. This track runs in parallel with\n  the phases below and is never checked off.\n- [x] **Phase 3 — Complex packing (5.2/5.3) + spatial differencing.** Unlocks most\n  HRRR fields. See the\n  \"Provider probe & selection\" component above for the full spec.\n\n  **Status (2026-07-27):** Python bindings (gribtract-py) and provider probe are\n  implemented. crates.io publish prep is complete (docs/notes/publish-guide.md,\n  dry-run verified), but the actual publish step requires a crates.io API token\n  — an ExternalSecret following the `crates-io-token-pdftract-externalsecret.yml.disabled`\n  pattern needs to be provisioned in declarative-config, then the publish sequence\n  in publish-guide.md must be run by a maintainer. Neither `gribtract` nor\n  `gribtract-core` is currently live on crates.io (verified via crates.io API).\n\n## Marathon loop contract\n\nFor an autonomous session to make safe, monotonic progress, each iteration must:\n1. Pick a corpus message currently failing (or absent) — the harness lists them.\n2. Add/confirm it as a fixture (real file, provenance recorded).\n3. Implement/repair the relevant template decoder.\n4. `cargo test` → full sampled differential suite passes; no regression vs the\n   ratcheted fixture set.\n5. Commit. The loop drives two coupled north-star metrics upward, **in this\n   priority**: (a) **agreement coverage** (% messages matching, by template) — the\n   gate; and (b) **decode throughput** (MB/s and speedup vs eccodes/wgrib2, plus\n   `stations × hours / sec` for point extraction) — the proof. A throughput gain\n   that lowers agreement is a regression, not progress. Both are published to the\n   proof-of-speed dashboard every iteration.\n\nSeparately from the phase work, the **point-extraction parse-speed track (Phase 2c)\nis an open-ended optimization loop**: keep trying new techniques to make station\nextraction faster, expect most attempts to fail or regress and back them out, and\nlog what didn't work so the loop doesn't repeat it. Dead ends are normal here — the\ncorrectness gate makes the exploration safe. When no template/correctness bead is\nthe obvious next pick, advancing this track is always valid work.\n\n## Open Questions\n\n- **Reference decoder of record:** eccodes (richer metadata) vs wgrib2 (ubiquitous\n  in NOAA tooling)? Likely eccodes primary, wgrib2 as a second cross-check.\n- **Tolerance derivation:** confirm that decimal/binary scale factors fully\n  determine representable precision for each packing template, or whether some\n  templates need an empirically-set band.\n- **Corpus governance:** fixtures are real grib2 — size/licensing/storage. CI wiring TBD.\n- **Scope of metadata naming:** ship a parameter/level name table, or expose raw\n  numeric ids and leave naming to the consumer initially?\n\n## ADR-1: 2026-07-20 — Add a wasm32 build target and a public, client-side interactive decode demo\n\n### Context\n\ngribtract's core value proposition, stated in the README, is \"no C toolchain, no\nFFI\" for the default build (DRT 5.0/5.2/5.3/5.41 — JPEG2000 is the one deliberate,\nfeature-gated exception). `gribtract-core` is already described in\n`docs/plan/plan.md` as \"no_std-friendly where able\" and has zero I/O dependencies —\nit takes `&[u8]` in, returns typed `Field`s out.\n\nDespite that, the only way anyone can currently *experience* gribtract is `git\nclone` + `cargo build`. The repo is public (6 GitHub stargazers as of 2026-07-20),\nnot yet published to crates.io (`bf-1pyo` closed its dry-run work but the actual\n`cargo publish` step is blocked on a maintainer-held crates.io token that does not\nexist on this box — flagged as a blocker below, not solved by this ADR), and the\nproof-of-speed dashboard (`dashboard.html` + `bench-results.json`, see \"Throughput &\nproof-of-speed dashboard\" above) only renders locally via `cargo xtask serve`. For a\nproject trying to earn adoption, \"clone a Rust workspace and compile it\" is a lot to\nask of someone evaluating whether gribtract solves their problem. There is currently\nno zero-install way to hand someone a `.grib2` file's worth of proof that this\nworks.\n\nMeanwhile, decode is demonstrably fast and self-contained (100+ MB/s on simple\npacking per `bench-results.json`, all reference-decoder-verified) and the crate\nboundary (`gribtract-core` → `gribtract`) already separates the pure-computation\npath from I/O concerns (`gribtract-fetch`) and from platform-specific bindings\n(`gribtract-py`). WebAssembly is a natural next target: it is, by construction, the\nstrictest possible \"no C toolchain, no FFI, no host filesystem\" execution\nenvironment — running gribtract-core in a browser tab is not just a demo gimmick,\nit is a forcing function that structurally enforces the project's core claim.\n\n### Decision\n\nAdd `wasm32-unknown-unknown` as a first-class, CI-checked build target for\n`gribtract-core` and `gribtract` (the pure-compute crates only — `gribtract-fetch`\nand `gribtract-py` are explicitly out of scope for wasm), via a new thin wrapper\ncrate `crates/gribtract-wasm` (wasm-bindgen bindings exposing `decode(bytes: &[u8])\n-> JsValue` and a lazy point-extraction call). Ship a small, self-contained static\nHTML page — same \"no external CDN at runtime, opens offline\" rule already\nestablished for `dashboard.html` in `docs/notes/throughput-dashboard.md` — that lets\na visitor drag a `.grib2` file onto the page and see it decoded live in their\nbrowser: a field inventory table plus a simple canvas heatmap of one selected\nfield's grid. No server, no upload, no install. This becomes the project's public\nfront door: the README's and repo's primary \"try it\" link, replacing \"clone and\n`cargo build --release`\" as the first thing an evaluator is asked to do.\n\nThis is implemented as follow-on beads (see below), not in this commit — this ADR\nrecords the decision to take the dependency-shape and target-support hit, and why.\n\n### Alternatives Considered\n\n1. **Status quo — Rust crate + CLI only.** Zero extra maintenance surface. Rejected\n   as insufficient for a public repo trying to earn adoption before it is even on\n   crates.io: the only path to \"does this work for my file?\" is a full Rust\n   toolchain and a `cargo build`, which is a high floor for a first impression.\n2. **Host only the existing proof-of-speed dashboard publicly, skip wasm.** Cheaper\n   — reuses `dashboard.html` as-is, and does prove the speed claim publicly. But it\n   is a *report*, not a *demo*: a visitor still cannot bring their own file and see\n   it decoded. Complementary, not a substitute — filed as its own bead\n   (`artifact-improvement`, \"publish the proof-of-speed dashboard as a live site\")\n   rather than folded into this decision.\n3. **Server-side decode API (upload a file, get JSON back) instead of client-side\n   wasm.** Rejected: reintroduces a server, hosting cost, and an upload/attack\n   surface for a project whose entire selling point is \"no dependencies, runs\n   anywhere.\" Client-side wasm keeps decode fully in the visitor's browser — zero\n   backend, zero file upload, consistent with \"pure-Rust, no C toolchain\" extended\n   one step further to \"no server, either.\"\n4. **Lead with the Python bindings (`gribtract-py`, already planned for Phase 7) as\n   the primary \"try it\" path instead.** Rejected as the *primary* surface — `pip\n   install` + a Python runtime is still real friction compared to a link that opens\n   in any browser. The PyO3 bindings remain valuable as a separate, already-planned\n   deliverable; they don't substitute for a zero-install public demo.\n\n### Consequences\n\n- New crate `crates/gribtract-wasm` added to the workspace (wasm-bindgen dependency,\n  `cdylib` crate-type, mirroring the existing `gribtract-py` pattern of an\n  optional/non-default workspace member so default `cargo build`/`cargo test`\n  behavior is unaffected).\n- `wasm32-unknown-unknown` becomes a second target the differential-harness\n  contract implicitly protects: `gribtract-core`'s \"no_std-friendly where able\"\n  note goes from aspirational to load-bearing. Any future dependency added to\n  `gribtract-core` or `gribtract` that breaks a `cargo build --target\n  wasm32-unknown-unknown -p gribtract` check is a regression, the same way a\n  differential-agreement drop is a regression.\n- Wasm binary size becomes a metric worth tracking (small today given\n  `gribtract-core`'s minimal dependency footprint) — a follow-on bead should add a\n  size check alongside the existing throughput/agreement metrics so it doesn't\n  silently creep.\n- Does **not** touch the correctness oracle or the Phase 2c parse-speed track: the\n  wasm target compiles the same `gribtract-core` source the differential harness\n  already verifies, so existing agreement guarantees carry over unchanged.  }\n165\t    }\n166\t\n167\t    /// Probe a single URL\n168\t    async fn probe_url(&mut self, provider: &str, url: &str) -> ProbeResult {\n169\t        let start = std::time::Instant::now();\n170\t\n171\t        match self.probe_url_inner(url).await {\n172\t            Ok(result) => {\n173\t                let _elapsed = start.elapsed();\n174\t                ProbeResult {\n175\t                    provider: provider.to_string(),\n176\t                    probe_url: url.to_string(),\n177\t                    connect_ms: result.connect_time.as_millis() as u64,\n178\t                    ttfb_ms: result.ttfb.as_millis() as u64,\n179\t                    throughput_mbs: result.throughput_mbs,\n180\t                    score: Self::calculate_score(&result),\n181\t                    success: true,\n182\t                    error: None,\n183\t                    timestamp: chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339(),\n184\t                }\n185\t            }\n186\t            Err(e) => {\n187\t                let _elapsed = start.elapsed();\n188\t                ProbeResult {\n189\t                    provider: provider.to_string(),\n190\t                    probe_url: url.to_string(),\n191\t                    connect_ms: _elapsed.as_millis() as u64,\n192\t                    ttfb_ms: _elapsed.as_millis() as u64,\n193\t                    throughput_mbs: 0.0,\n194\t                    score: f64::MAX,\n195\t                    success: false,\n196\t                    error: Some(e.to_string()),\n197\t                    timestamp: chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339(),\n198\t                }\n199\t            }\n200\t        }\n201\t    }\n202\t\n203\t    /// Inner probe logic for a single URL\n204\t    async fn probe_url_inner(&mut self, url: &str) -> Result<ProbeInnerResult, crate::FetchError> {\n205\t        let _start = std::time::Instant::now();\n206\t\n207\t        // Use the client's probe method to get basic connection info\n208\t        let probe_info = self.client.probe(url).await?;\n209\t        let connect_time = probe_info.connect_time;\n210\t\n211\t        // Check if range requests are supported\n212\t        let supports_range = probe_info.supports_range;\n213\t\n214\t        // Get content length\n215\t        let content_length = probe_info.content_length.unwrap_or(0);\n216\t\n217\t        // Now do a small range request to measure TTFB and throughput\n218\t        let range_start = std::time::Instant::now();\n219\t\n220\t        let range_response = if supports_range && content_length > 1024 {\n221\t            Some(self.client.fetch_head(url, 1024).await?)\n222\t        } else {\n223\t            None\n224\t        };\n225\t\n226\t        let ttfb = range_start.elapsed();\n227\t\n228\t        let throughput_mbs = if let Some(resp) = range_response {\n229\t            let bytes = resp.data.len() as f64;\n230\t            let seconds = ttfb.as_secs_f64();\n231\t            (bytes / seconds) / (1024.0 * 1024.0)\n232\t        } else {\n233\t            0.0\n234\t        };\n235\t\n236\t        Ok(ProbeInnerResult {\n237\t            connect_time,\n238\t            ttfb,\n239\t            throughput_mbs,\n240\t        })\n241\t    }\n242\t\n243\t    /// Calculate a combined score for provider selection\n244\t    ///\n245\t    /// Lower is better. Formula: connect_ms + ttfb_ms + (1 / throughput_mbs)\n246\t    fn calculate_score(result: &ProbeInnerResult) -> f64 {\n247\t        let connect_penalty = result.connect_time.as_millis() as f64;\n248\t        let ttfb_penalty = result.ttfb.as_millis() as f64;\n249\t        let throughput_penalty = if result.throughput_mbs > 0.0 {\n250\t            1000.0 / result.throughput_mbs\n251\t        } else {\n252\t            10000.0 // Large penalty for no throughput\n253\t        };\n254\t\n255\t        connect_penalty + ttfb_penalty + throughput_penalty\n256\t    }\n257\t\n258\t    /// Get the current git SHA for reproducibility\n259\t    fn get_git_sha() -> Option<String> {\n260\t        std::process::Command::new(\"git\")\n261\t            .args([\"rev-parse\", \"HEAD\"])\n262\t            .output()\n263\t            .ok()\n264\t            .and_then(|output| {\n265\t                let sha = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout).trim().to_string();\n266\t                if !sha.is_empty() {\n267\t                    Some(sha)\n268\t                } else {\n269\t                    None\n270\t                }\n271\t            })\n272\t    }\n273\t\n274\t    /// Get ProbeResult> {\n279\t        results.models.get(model).and_then(|model_results| {\n280\t            model_results.iter().find(|r| r.success)\n281\t        })\n282\t    }\n283\t\n284\t    /// Write Err(_) => true, // Invalid timestamp means stale\n306\t        }\n307\t    }\n308\t\n309\t    /// Record a failure for the given provider\n310\t    ///\n311\t    /// Increments the consecutive failure Providers should be re-probed in three cases:\n//! 1. **File absent**: `ProviderProbe::load` returns `Err`\n//! 2. **File stale**: `is_fresh()` returns `false` (timestamp > 24h old)\n//! 3. **Consecutive HTTP errors**: `ProviderFailureTracker::should_reprobe()` returns `true`\n//!\n//! u32, d: u32) -> Option<i64> {\n    if !(1..=12).contains(&m) || !(1..=31).contains(&d) {\n        return None;\n    }\n    // Hinnant civil_from_days inverse:\n    // shift year so March = month 0\n    let (y, m) = if m <= 2 { (y - 1, m + 9) } else { (y, m - 3) };\n    let era = if y >= 0 { y } else { y - 399 } / 400;\n    let yoe = y - era * 400; // [0, 399]\n    let doy = (153 * m as i64 + 2) / 5 / 365)\n        let mut year = 1970 + (days / 365) as i32;\n\n        // Adjust for leap years\n        loop {\n            let days_in_year = if is_leap_year(year) { 366 } else { 365 };\n fn is_leap_year(year: i32) -> bool {\n        (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || (year % 400 == 0)\n    }\n\n    fn day_of_year_to_md(day_of_year: u32, year: i32) -> (u32, u32) {\n        let days_in_month = if is_leap_year(year) {\n            [0, 31, 29, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]\n        } else {\n            [0, 31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]\n        };\n\n        let mut day = day_of_year + 1; // 1-indexed\n        let mut month = 1;\n\n        while month <= 12 && day > days_in_month[month as usize] {\n            day -= days_in_month[month as usize];\n            month += 1;\n        }\n\n        (month, day)\n    }\n\n    #[test]\n    fn ymd_to_days_known() {\n        // 1970-01-01 = day 0\n        assert_eq!(ymd_to_days(1970, 1, 1),
